coverageNote: Enumerated from disk: 8 unit directories containing an *-index.md (the domain root plus 23.01-23.07), 45 .md files total - exactly the expected 8 units / 45 files. Every file was read in full through the 3a->3b->3c cycle; no sampling. The two leaf feature files at the domain root (23.08, 23.09) were audited as part of the domain-root unit. Cross-references were followed outside the domain before calling anything missing: moscow-ledger.md (to confirm 23.06.01 / 23.06.05 / 23.09 are Won't, so their deliberately-unspecified Behavior/States are correct rather than gaps), 01.06.02-credit-backed-portfolio.md D-06 (finding #010), and 01.04.03-treasury-mandate.md Behavior (finding #013). Scoring: dimensions 2 (Persona Specificity), 4 (Constraint Explicitness) and 6 (Competitive Positioning) are marked N/A on every unit - personas, constraints and competitive landscape are owned by meta/personas.md, meta/constraints.md and meta/competitive-landscape.md, which these units correctly reference rather than restate. That leaves 5 rubric checkpoints per unit (dims 1, 3, 5, 7, 8) plus one added checkpoint per blocking implementer-simulation gap, per scoring.md ('Gaps found during Implementer Simulation are added directly to the punch list as ❌ items and also count toward the ambiguity score'). Dimension 7 scored ✅ on all eight units: every row in every formal Open Questions table carries an owner and a deferral target, and resolved rows are struck through with a cited source. A systemic issue was considered and deliberately NOT reported as a finding in its own right: 20 inline '[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]' markers survive in edge-case cells across the domain although Step 5 has run and closed (stated explicitly at 23.01.03 Q-03 and 23.01.05 Q-01). Most are covered by a properly-tracked Open Question in the same or parent file, so per the audit rules they are tracked deferral, not findings; the two whose substance is genuinely uncovered are reported as findings #009 and #011 on their merits rather than as marker defects. Devil's-advocate pass dropped 9 raw candidates: (a) the '5 merges' vs 9 merged-candidate rows arithmetic in career-finance-business-index.md D-02 (narrative history, not build-affecting); (b) 23.09's Behavior/States [PENDING] (MoSCoW = Won't, so correct); (c) 23.09 Q-02 deferred to MoSCoW after MoSCoW ran (answered, just not struck); (d) the undefined 'reconciliation window' at 23.01.01:46 (timing policy, downstream per the retry-policy exclusion); (e) 23.03.03's Day 3 / Day 14 ladder configurability (a concrete default is given; configurability is FE spec); (f) 23.02.04's UK-Germany happy path (its Q-02 explicitly tracks the corridor re-pointing); (g) the domain-root Role Matrix rollups vs child matrices (all are documented rollups with explanatory notes); (h) 23.02.01's Role Lens calling the mobile surface open while its own Q-01 records it resolved (behaviour is identical either way); (i) 23.02-cx CX-04's broken '(see Q-01)' pointer to a rules-substrate question no Q-01 covers (the substance is explicitly labelled an architecture question, which the vision layer does not owe).

findings.claim: 23.08's stated core value - telling a user their existing insurance does not cover professional use - has no specified input path, and the feature simultaneously forbids guessing. Nothing in the domain lets the platform learn what cover a user already holds.
findings.evidence: 23.08-point-of-need-insurance.md:78 — 'D-03 | Telling a user their existing cover does not apply is the feature's real value | See DT-03 — even though it may end in no referral'. 23.08-point-of-need-insurance.md:62 (DT-03) — 'the common case is not "no policy" — it is a **home contents policy that excludes professional use**. The musician believes they are covered; they are not' … '✅ CONFIRMED, and it changes the feature's job: the value is **telling someone their existing cover does not apply**, not selling them a new policy.' But 23.08-point-of-need-insurance.md:37 requires — 'The offer is wrong for them (already covered, ineligible, wrong territory) | … | Suppressible; never nagging. **The trigger must be a fact, not a guess**', and :38 — 'Cover status must be unambiguous, never implied by having seen an offer'. The Behavior section (:23) sources trigger data only from what the platform already holds — 'A trigger event produces a contextual offer with the data the platform already holds — the instrument, its value, the tour dates, the venue's requirement'. Cross-Cut Notes (:66-70) list Gear Registry (15), 13/16/17/18 triggers, and 23.04.01 as a *destination* for policies bought through the platform — no source for pre-existing external cover. None of Q-01 (product vs monetisation), Q-02 (broker regulation) or Q-03 (which shard owns the trigger) covers it.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether D-03 is delivered as a per-user determination (requiring a policy-declaration or policy-upload intake that no file specifies) or as a generic class-level warning ('home policies usually exclude professional use'). The first needs a data-capture flow and an eligibility model; the second is a static banner. Two implementers reading D-03 plus the no-guessing edge case build materially different features.

findings.claim: 23.01.05 lists 'advance' as an income type carried on the ledger row, while the domain CX, 23.01.02 and 23.06.01 all state that an advance is a liability that must never become an income row. Both statements are unmarked; they cannot both hold.
findings.evidence: 23.01.05-income-to-work-linkage.md:25 — 'For each linked work the projection presents three things, and only these three: a **total to date**, a **breakdown by income type** (the income type is carried on the ledger row by the emitting domain — session fee, royalty line, sync fee, backend/points, **advance**), and a **timeline** of when each event settled.' Against: career-finance-business-cx.md:85 (CX-04) — 'an advance is a **liability** that looks exactly like income when it lands in a bank account, and if 23.01.02 imports it as income, three artefacts are wrong at once (tax pack, proof-of-earnings, runway)'; career-finance-business-cx.md:90 — 'Liabilities and income are separate records, never merged. An imported credit that is actually an advance must **net rather than count**'; 23.01.02-off-platform-income-import.md:42 — 'A bank credit is a **loan or an advance**, not income | Same problem, higher stakes — an advance is a liability, and 23.06.03 must net it, not count it | Routed to advances, not income'; 23.06.01-advance-underwriting-offers.md:23 — 'An accepted advance creates a recoupment position (`#CX-02`) and is recorded as a **liability, never as income**'; 23.06-advances-commission-recoupment-cx.md:48 — 'The advance is a liability record; income events are facts. Never merged.' 23.01.05 is also internally incoherent on this: the same paragraph (:25) says 'Because a work can be advanced against (23.06.03), every figure is shown as **two numbers — gross and net-to-me**' — i.e. the advance is what makes net-to-me smaller than gross, which is a deduction, not an income type in the same breakdown.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the emitting domain's income_type enum on a ledger row includes an 'advance' member. Including it puts advance money into gross income, which by the domain's own analysis simultaneously corrupts the tax pack (23.02.03), the proof-of-earnings artefact (23.01.04) and the runway forecast (23.06.04). Excluding it leaves 23.01.05's per-work breakdown with no way to render advance money against a work at all. An implementer must invent the resolution and there is no tracked question covering it.

findings.claim: For two platform emitters describing one economic fact, neither which emitter wins nor whether the merge is automatic is decidable: 'the platform-authoritative event' is undefined when both events are platform events, and the described high-confidence path performs an automatic link that D-04 says never happens.
findings.evidence: 23.01.01-income-event-ledger.md:43 — 'Two platform emitters describe the **same economic fact** (e.g. a settlement event *and* a payout event for one payment) with **different** idempotency keys | Reconciliation on (owning identity, amount, economic-date window, counterparty): **the platform-authoritative event (D-02) is kept**, the other is linked as a corroborating reference, not a second income row. If confidence is below the **auto-merge threshold**, both are held and the user is asked to confirm … | **At most a "we linked two records of the same payment" note**; if ambiguous, a confirm-merge prompt'. D-02 (:95) says only 'The ledger is a subscriber, not a mover of money' — it establishes no precedence between a domain-17 settlement event and a payments-cross-cut payout event, and both are platform-authoritative under it. Against the automatic half: 23.01.01-income-event-ledger.md:97 — 'D-04 | **Reconciliation proposes, never silently auto-merges** | See DT-04 — a wrong auto-merge deletes real income that flows into the tax pack and proof-of-earnings; **the platform-authoritative event wins the tie**' (D-04's own context is the platform-vs-platform tie, so it is in scope). Q-04 (:108) tracks only the numeric boundary — 'For the reconciliation confidence threshold (D-04), what is the auto-merge vs ask boundary … The precise rule is a downstream contract decision but the *policy* (bias toward asking) is locked here' — it does not name the emitter-precedence rule, and 'bias toward asking' conflicts with 'at most a note'.
findings.forcedInvention: (a) Which emitter outranks the other when both are platform sources — the choice determines the surviving row's source domain label and counterparty, both of which are user-visible in the source breakdown and the tax pack's 'income by source' section. (b) Whether the high-confidence path suppresses the second row automatically with a passive note, or still requires a confirm-merge. Two implementers split on both.

findings.claim: v1 is locked to US-only, yet the only concrete deduction-category vocabulary anywhere in domain 23 is a UK one, presented as the feature's happy path. No US category set exists in the tree, and the file's own rule for an unsupported jurisdiction is to refuse to operate.
findings.evidence: 23.02.02-deduction-categorization-jurisdiction-rules.md:27-28 (Happy Path) — '1. Musician declares **UK sole-trader jurisdiction**. 2. Their capture surface offers a **UK-shaped vocabulary: equipment, instruments, rehearsal, travel, subsistence, home-studio use, professional fees**.' Against, in the same file, last-updated the same day (2026-07-23): 23.02.02:83 Q-01 — 'is **RESOLVED — the United States only**, per ideation-index.md **D-32** … so **v1 encodes US musician/sole-trader rules alone**'; and 23.02.02:38 — 'Jurisdiction not supported | **Must fail honestly** — a generic category list dressed as a rule set is worse than nothing | Explicit "not supported; export raw data instead" rather than a plausible-looking wrong answer', reinforced by D-02 (:76) 'Unsupported jurisdictions fail honestly rather than degrading to a generic list'. Parent 23.02-expenses-tax-readiness-index.md:48 states the same lock: 'v1 encodes US sole-trader (Schedule C) rules and nothing else'. A grep across all 45 files of domain 23 for 'Schedule C' returns only two Open-Question rows (23.02-index:48 and 23.02.03:97) and no category list; the UK list at 23.02.02:28 is the only enumerated vocabulary in the domain.
findings.forcedInvention: The entire US deduction-category vocabulary that 23.02.01's capture surface must offer in v1 — because CX-01 states 'The jurisdiction's rule set **defines** the category vocabulary available at capture; capture cannot offer a neutral category list' (23.02-expenses-tax-readiness-cx.md:10) and DT-01 rejects shipping jurisdiction-neutral. The implementer must invent the Schedule C category set, plus the US capital threshold, US mileage/per-diem rates and US home-office apportionment test that D-01's tax-year-versioned rules pin to. Taken literally the happy path is also unsatisfiable in v1: step 1 declares a jurisdiction that step :38 requires the product to refuse.

findings.claim: The behaviour when a withholding reclaim succeeds and the refund arrives is explicitly left unmodelled, with the two candidate models named and neither chosen, and no owner or deferral target attached.
findings.evidence: 23.02.04-cross-border-withholding-reclaim.md:44 — 'Reclaim succeeds; refund arrives | **A new income event? A negative deduction?** It restates a possibly-filed year (`#CX-03`) | **Must be modelled explicitly, not improvised**'. There is no [PENDING] marker, no owner and no stage on this row. None of the file's Open Questions covers it: Q-01 (:85) is whether the feature reaches into booking (17) for relief at source, Q-02 (:86) is which treaty corridors launch, Q-03 (:87) is whether WeJammin is itself a withholding agent. The parent CX only restates the problem — 23.02-expenses-tax-readiness-cx.md:68 — 'A reclaim filed and refunded changes the credit position for a year that may already be filed.' The nearest domain-level acknowledgement is itself untracked: career-finance-business-cx.md:47 — 'A reversal must propagate everywhere … **Reversal is the domain's hardest transition** and it is under-specified at breadth in every child.'
findings.forcedInvention: Whether a successful reclaim refund is (a) a new income event on the ledger, (b) a negative deduction reversing the original withholding line on the original income row, or (c) something else. The choice is not cosmetic: option (a) increases gross income in the refund year and inflates the proof-of-earnings verified total; option (b) restates the original year's gross/deductions/net and therefore forces a superseding tax pack under CX-06's supersede-and-notify path. It also determines whether 23.01.03 D-03 ('gross, deductions and net on one row convert at one rate/date') is violated, since the refund arrives at a different FX rate than the original withholding.

findings.claim: The sub-domain is scoped by D-02 to off-platform work only, with an explicit test ('did the money move through WeJammin? If yes, no invoice exists'), yet Operator settlement shortfalls and deposits — which arise from on-platform domain 17 flows — are assigned to 23.03.02 and 23.03.03. The 23.03/17 boundary is nowhere tracked.
findings.evidence: 23.03-invoicing-receivables-index.md:39 — 'D-02 | Scope is **off-platform work**; on-platform work is paid by the payments/escrow cross-cut and never invoiced | … **The boundary is: did the money move through WeJammin? If yes, no invoice exists.**' Enforced at 23.03.02-invoice-issuance-compliance.md:43 — 'Invoice for work already paid through WeJammin | **Should be impossible — parent D-02** | Blocked with an explanation'. Against: 23.03.02-invoice-issuance-compliance.md:18 (Operator Role Lens) — 'Issues for room hire and **settlement shortfalls**'; 23.03.03-payment-chasing-dunning-aging.md:18 — 'Chases **deposits and settlement shortfalls**, and is simultaneously the ecosystem's archetypal slow payer'; 23.03.03-payment-chasing-dunning-aging.md:71 (Cross-Cut Notes) — 'Touches **17 Live Booking & Settlement** — **settlement shortfalls are receivables**, and the promoter is both counterparty and future employer.' Deposits are separately assigned to 17 elsewhere: 23.03-invoicing-receivables-cx.md:56 — 'Operator less so — their protection is a **deposit taken up front (domain 17)**, a mechanism they already have.' Q-01 (:46) tracks only the 05 Services Marketplace boundary; no question names 17.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether an Operator's shortfall on a settlement that ran through WeJammin's own payments cross-cut produces an invoice and enters the 23.03.03 dunning ladder, or is refused by 23.03.02's D-02 block and handled entirely inside 17. The two builds differ in which sub-domain owns the receivable, which aging buckets it appears in, and whether the ladder ever fires against an on-platform counterparty.

findings.claim: 23.03.02 is named for its compliance fields but enumerates only VAT/GST and reverse-charge treatment — a regime that does not exist in the locked US-only launch market. The US invoice compliance field set the feature actually needs in v1 is specified nowhere.
findings.evidence: 23.03.02-invoice-issuance-compliance.md:39 — 'User is **VAT/GST registered** mid-year | Treatment changes prospectively; historic invoices do not move | Prospective only'; :41 — 'Reverse charge / cross-border B2B VAT | Jurisdiction-specific and genuinely hard | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` — depends on 23.02.02's jurisdiction rules'; DT-03 (:63) reasons from 'a **UK sole trader below the VAT threshold**'. Against: 23.02-expenses-tax-readiness-index.md:50 (Q-03) — 'Scope-narrowed by **D-32** (US-only launch): **there is no US VAT/GST**, and state marketplace-facilitator sales tax is provider-handled and explicitly not built (`meta/constraints.md` § Compliance).' The only compliance fields the file actually locks are jurisdiction-neutral: sequential numbering (D-01/D-02) and the PO number (D-03). Behavior (:23) defers the rest — 'Fields are pre-filled from the user's tax profile (23.02.02)' — but 23.02.02 encodes no US field set either (see finding #004). The [PENDING] marker's stage has run and closed (stated at 23.01.03 Q-03), and the row carries no owner.
findings.forcedInvention: Which identifiers and treatments a compliant v1 US invoice must carry — TIN/EIN presentation, W-9 exchange with the payer, any state sales-tax line — none of which appear in domain 23. An implementer building v1 from this file would either ship a VAT-shaped invoice that no US filer needs, or invent the US field set unaided.

findings.claim: The sub-domain CX asserts that term confirmation is mandatory before an extraction may drive an alert, while the same CX file and the owning feature both require unconfirmed dates to alert anyway.
findings.evidence: 23.04-deal-contract-vault-cx.md:31 (CX-01, synthesis Q2) — 'Trigger chain: Upload → extract → user confirms each term. **Confirmation is mandatory, not optional: an unconfirmed extraction must never silently drive an alert or a reconciliation finding.**' Against, in the same file: 23.04-deal-contract-vault-cx.md:51 (CX-02, synthesis Q5) — 'A date passing while the extraction is still unconfirmed — **the alert must fire anyway**, flagged as unconfirmed. **Silence is the one unacceptable outcome.**' And in the owning feature: 23.04.03-option-reversion-obligation-alerts.md:86 — 'D-02 | **Unconfirmed dates alert anyway, flagged** | Silence is the only unacceptable outcome'; :45 — 'Extraction unconfirmed when the date approaches | **Fire anyway**, flagged as unconfirmed'; :61 (States → Partial) — 'Unconfirmed dates alert anyway, flagged'. Note the reconciliation half is consistent and confirms the alert half is the outlier: 23.04.04-deal-to-rights-reconciliation.md:78 — 'D-02 | **Only confirmed terms reconcile**', and 23.04.02-key-term-extraction-deal-summary.md:23 narrows the prohibition to reconciliation only — 'Unconfirmed extractions are visibly provisional and must never silently drive a **reconciliation finding**' — saying nothing about alerts.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the alert scheduler gates on confirmation state. A downstream IA writer working from the CX synthesis (which is what CX files exist to supply) builds the gate and ships a vault that stays silent on an unconfirmed reversion date — the exact outcome 23.04.03 calls 'the catastrophic failure' at :44. The 'silently' / 'flagged' qualifier partially reconciles the two, but 'Confirmation is mandatory, not optional' is stated as an absolute and is simply false for alerts.

findings.claim: 23.04.03 quantifies the alert lead-time band for one of its three term classes and leaves the other two as unmeasurable prose, in a feature whose own D-01 makes lead time the design's governing quantity.
findings.evidence: 23.04.03-option-reversion-obligation-alerts.md:27 — '**Lead-time bands scale with the action.** A reversion (needs a lawyer + a letter) schedules alerts at roughly **6 months, 3 months, 1 month, on-open, and inside the window**. An option exercise (needs a decision, maybe a call) schedules **weeks out**. An operator lease break / insurance renewal schedules on **a generic calendar interval**. The bands are seeded per term-type at extraction time (23.04.02) and are user-adjustable.' The file sets its own precision bar by quantifying the reversion band, then abandons it. D-01 (:85) — 'Over-alert deliberately; **lead time scales with the action required** | See DT-01 — the risk is asymmetric and so is the design' — makes the unquantified bands load-bearing, and CX-02 (23.04-deal-contract-vault-cx.md:38) states the asymmetry that makes them consequential: 'a false alert costs a minute of attention; a **missed** alert costs a catalogue, permanently.' A missed option window is the second-highest-value date class in the sub-domain (Role Lens :16-17). No Open Question covers the seeding values: Q-01 is resolved (route to action), Q-02 is event-triggered-date sequencing, Q-03 is export-on-departure.
findings.forcedInvention: The concrete option-exercise and operator-renewal alert schedules. 'Weeks out' spans 2 to 12 weeks and 'a generic calendar interval' is undecidable; two implementers seed materially different schedules for dates the file itself says are unrecoverable when missed.

findings.claim: 23.05.02 specifies a Fan-readable public milestone timeline — the only Fan access cell in the whole of domain 23 — while the same file's resolved Q-01, and the domain-01 decision it cites, state that no public artist timeline exists and that a timeline may never be rendered on any public surface.
findings.evidence: The public timeline is asserted as behaviour: 23.05.02-auto-milestone-timeline.md:23 — 'Each milestone has a private form (complete, factual) and a **public projection** (curated, artist-controlled). The two are one entity with a visibility rule'; :30 (Happy Path step 4) — 'The Musician toggles it public; **it joins their artist profile story (01/20)**'; :19 (Fan Role Lens) — 'Fan | Read-only | **The only `👁️` a Fan holds in domain 23.** An artist's public timeline is fan-facing content — the story of the act. **They see the public projection**'; and the parent Role Matrix note, 23.05-career-progression-benchmarking-index.md:32 — '**Fan is `👁️ Read-only` on the milestone timeline** … because **an artist's public timeline (first show, first release, the record that broke) is fan-facing content**, not private finance.' Against, in the same feature file: 23.05.02-auto-milestone-timeline.md:85 (Q-01, RESOLVED) — '**Its premise is false: 01/20 render no public career timeline for this to be.** `01.06.02` **D-06** — "The portfolio never claims completeness, and **never renders chronological density on a public surface — no activity graph, no per-year counts, no timeline spine**…" — with the public-rendering table row "Per-year credit density / activity timeline · ❌ **Never** (D-06, DT-07)" … and **domain 20 has no artist career-timeline surface**.' Verified at source rather than via the quote: 01-identity-profiles-organizations/01.06-portfolio-media-epk/01.06.02-credit-backed-portfolio.md:68 — '| Per-year credit density / activity timeline | ❌ **Never** (D-06, DT-07) |' and :215 — 'D-06 | **The portfolio never claims completeness, and never renders chronological density on a public surface** — no activity graph, no per-year counts, no timeline spine'. A grep for 'career timeline' across 20-fanbase-direct-to-fan/ returns nothing.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the public projection exists at all, and if so on which surface it renders. Both candidate owners disclaim it — 01.06.02 D-06 bans a timeline on any public surface it controls, and 20 has no such surface — so an implementer must either invent a third public surface for it, or build 23.05.02 with no public projection and no Fan access, which contradicts the parent Role Matrix's only Fan cell. Every artefact that depends on the public/private split (D-02 'one entity, one visibility rule', D-03 'income-derived milestones default private, hard', DT-03's 'central design problem') resolves differently under the two readings.

findings.claim: The minimum cohort size is elevated to a hard, enforced privacy control and a numbered decision, but no value is stated anywhere — and that value alone determines whether the feature ever renders.
findings.evidence: 23.05.03-peer-cohort-benchmarking.md:23 (Behavior) — 'Benchmarks are **aggregates with a minimum cohort size**, below which nothing is shown at all.' :37 — 'Cohort is too small | **Re-identification.** Four session drummers in one city is four named people; one of them can work out the others' rates | **Hard minimum cohort size, enforced.** Show nothing rather than something. **This is a privacy control, not a UX preference**'. :80 — 'D-03 | **Hard minimum cohort size, enforced; show nothing below it** | Small cohorts are named individuals'. No number appears in the file or anywhere in the domain (verified by grep for 'minimum cohort' across all 45 files: three hits, none carrying a value). The threshold governs whether the product renders at all — :51 (States → Empty) — '"Not enough comparable data" — and **this will be the normal state for a long time**'. The three Open Questions do not set it: Q-01 (:88) is who sees benchmarks, Q-02 (:89) is the 22 Analytics boundary, Q-03 (:90) is consent opt-in. The one inline marker that is adjacent — :43 '`[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` — how many dimensions before the cohort is too small to show?' — asks about cohort dimensionality, not the size floor, points at a stage that has already run and closed, and carries no owner.
findings.forcedInvention: The k value. The file's own worked example implies k > 4, but k=5 and k=30 produce entirely different products: at k=5 the feature renders for most London session drummers and is arguably re-identifiable; at k=30 it renders for almost nobody at launch, which by the file's own framing turns the empty state into the permanent state and moots the feature. Because D-03 calls it a privacy control rather than a tuning parameter, it is not safely deferrable to a downstream layer.

findings.claim: 23.06.02 D-02 states two different behaviours for the same input in one line — ambiguous commission scope both defaults to a narrowest reading and holds the row — and 'narrowest defensible reading' is untestable as written.
findings.evidence: 23.06.02-commission-representation-deductions.md:79 — 'D-02 | **Scope defaults to the narrowest defensible reading; ambiguity holds the row** | See DT-02 — consolidation must not become a transfer to managers'. The edge case gives only the hold half: :38 — 'Commission scope is ambiguous (does "music income" include a gear sale? a teaching hour?) | Contracts are frequently vague on exactly the income classes this platform newly makes visible … | **Must refuse to guess. An unresolved scope holds the row rather than deducting wrongly**'; and States → Partial (:54) — 'Rule scope unresolved | **Row held, flagged; never deducted on a guess**'. DT-02 (:61) states both together — 'it argues for scope **defaulting to the narrowest defensible reading** with anything ambiguous **held rather than deducted**' — without naming the boundary between them. Nothing in the domain defines 'defensible': the contract terms feeding this come from 23.04.02, whose own rule for a contested clause is to refuse rather than pick (23.04.02:38 — 'Must refuse rather than pick: "we cannot determine this — read this clause" beats a confident guess'). Q-01 is resolved by D-02 itself, Q-02 is routing, Q-03 is the manager-as-user question — none defines the boundary.
findings.forcedInvention: For a 2019 management agreement reading 'all music income' against a 2026 gear-marketplace sale, whether the system (a) applies the narrow reading — excludes the gear sale, computes commission on the unambiguous classes, and pays out — or (b) holds the entire income row unnetted until the user resolves the scope. Option (a) pays the musician now and risks under-deducting; option (b) blocks their money. The user-visible outcome and the money differ, and no test distinguishes 'a narrow reading is available' from 'this is ambiguous'.

findings.claim: 23.07.03 states two mutually exclusive 'exactly three shapes' enumerations for the band distribution rule — one in its own Behavior section, a different one in its own resolved Q-02 quoting the owning spec — and the owning spec (01.04.03) confirms the second.
findings.evidence: 23.07.03-band-treasury-member-distribution.md:29-32 (Behavior, waterfall step 3) — '**Remainder divides by the distribution rule** — one of three shapes agreed by the band, ideally on day one (D-03): • **Equal** — remainder ÷ N members. • **Weighted** — fixed percentages per member summing to 100%. • **Per-role** — shares keyed to role/contribution (e.g. touring members vs. writers), still summing to 100%.' Against, in the same file, last-updated the same day (2026-07-23): 23.07.03:102 (Q-02, RESOLVED) — 'The rule's shapes are fixed by [01.04.03] Behavior: "**exactly three shapes: equal (split N ways), by income share (the percentages fixed in 01.04.01), or manual per event**".' The parent index repeats the second enum as the resolution: 23.07-budgeting-project-tour-pl-index.md:48 (Q-03, RESOLVED) — '01.04.03 Treasury Mandate's Behavior fixes the resulting rule to "exactly three shapes: **equal** (split N ways), **by income share** (the percentages fixed in 01.04.01), or **manual per event**".' Verified at source: 01-identity-profiles-organizations/01.04-band-ensemble-governance/01.04.03-treasury-mandate.md:25 — 'The distribution rule is one of **exactly three shapes**: **equal** (split N ways), **by income share** (the percentages fixed in 01.04.01), or **manual per event** (the mandate holder proposes a split, members see it, and — above the spend ceiling — governance's threshold from 01.04.01 must clear it). A band picks one default rule; a single inbound event may override to `manual` when the split is bespoke (a guest player on one gig).' Note that 23.07.03 Q-01 (:101) flags a *different* live tension with 01.04.03 (position-vs-balance) and explicitly tracks it; the enum divergence is flagged nowhere.
findings.forcedInvention: Which three-member enum the distribution engine implements. 'Per-role' exists only in 23.07.03 and is forbidden by the owning spec's 'exactly three shapes'; 'manual per event' — which 01.04.03 binds to a spend-ceiling and a governance threshold from 01.04.01 — is absent from 23.07.03's waterfall entirely. Building 23.07.03's enum yields a distribution shape the band-governance domain will not record and omits the per-event override 01.04.03 mandates; building 01.04.03's enum leaves 23.07.03's Behavior section describing a rule the product does not have. Because the waterfall's step 3 is what actually pays five people, the divergence is money.
